name: Technical SEO
summary: Crawling, indexing, site architecture, Core Web Vitals and structured data — the foundations that decide whether good content can rank.
heroTitle: Technical SEO that removes what's quietly holding rankings back.
heroIntro: If Google can't crawl, render or understand your pages, the best content in your market won't rank. I find the technical issues that actually cost you visibility and help your team fix them in the right order.
problem: Most technical problems are invisible from the front end. Pages look fine to visitors while Google wastes crawl budget on parameter URLs, ignores canonicals, or indexes staging pages instead of the real ones.
The usual audit makes this worse: a 300-row export of warnings with no sense of which ones matter. Technical SEO should end in a short list of changes your developers understand and can ship.

covers.title: Crawling & indexing
covers.body: Robots rules, sitemaps, canonicals, noindex logic, index bloat and the Search Console coverage reports that show what Google kept.

covers.title: Site architecture
covers.body: URL structure, click depth, faceted and paginated pages, and how authority flows through navigation and internal links.

covers.title: Rendering & JavaScript SEO
covers.body: Checking what Googlebot actually sees on React, Next.js, Vue and other JavaScript-heavy sites.

covers.title: Core Web Vitals
covers.body: LCP, INP and CLS diagnosis with specific fixes for images, fonts, scripts and layout shifts.

covers.title: Structured data
covers.body: Schema that matches visible content — Organization, Product, Article, FAQ, Breadcrumb and more — validated and monitored.

covers.title: Migrations & redesigns
covers.body: Redirect mapping, pre-launch checks and post-launch monitoring so a new site doesn't reset years of rankings.

process.title: Discover
process.body: Understand the business model, audience and revenue goals, then look at where technical health fits into them.

process.title: Diagnose
process.body: Audit what's there now against search data, competitors and how Google is actually treating the site.

process.title: Prioritise
process.body: Turn findings into a roadmap ranked by impact, effort and business value — not by how many issues a tool flags.

process.title: Implement & measure
process.body: Ship the work with your team, then track rankings, traffic, conversions and leads to decide what comes next.

deliverables: Prioritised technical audit with impact and effort for each issue
Core Web Vitals report with page-template level fixes
commonProblems: Pages marked 'Crawled – currently not indexed' in Search Console
Duplicate URLs from filters, parameters or trailing slashes
Traffic drop after a redesign, migration or CMS change
JavaScript content that Google renders late or not at all
Slow templates failing Core Web Vitals on mobile
whoFor: Sites with thousands of URLs where small technical issues compound
Teams planning a migration, replatform or redesign
JavaScript-framework sites that aren't ranking as they should
Businesses whose content is strong but traffic has plateaued

useCases.title: Pre-migration planning
useCases.body: Mapping every URL that earns traffic or links before a CMS move, then checking redirects and indexing daily after launch.

useCases.title: Index bloat cleanup
useCases.body: Reducing thousands of thin or duplicate URLs so Google spends its crawl on the pages that make money.

faqs.q: How long does a technical SEO audit take?
faqs.a: For most sites, two to four weeks from access to a prioritised roadmap. Very large or JavaScript-heavy sites take longer because rendering and log analysis need more time.

faqs.q: Do you implement the fixes or just recommend them?
faqs.a: Both are possible. I write developer-ready tickets and work with your team, and I can implement directly on platforms like WordPress, Shopify and Webflow.

faqs.q: Will fixing technical issues increase traffic on its own?
faqs.a: Sometimes significantly — especially when pages weren't being indexed. More often, technical work removes a ceiling so content and authority work can deliver results.

name: On-Page SEO
summary: Search intent, keyword mapping, content optimisation, metadata and internal links — making each page the best answer for the query it targets.
heroTitle: On-page SEO that matches each page to what searchers actually want.
heroIntro: Rankings are won page by page. I align every important page with one clear search intent, tighten the content around it, and connect it to the rest of your site so Google understands where it fits.
problem: Many sites target the same keyword with three different pages, or target a commercial keyword with an informational article. Both confuse Google and split your ranking potential.
On-page SEO is not stuffing keywords into headings. It's making sure the page answers the query better, more clearly and more completely than what currently ranks.

covers.title: Search intent analysis
covers.body: Reading the current results to understand what format, depth and angle Google rewards for each query.

covers.title: Keyword mapping
covers.body: One primary topic per page, supporting terms mapped, and cannibalisation removed.

covers.title: Content optimisation
covers.body: Restructuring sections, filling topical gaps and improving clarity without rewriting what already works.

covers.title: Titles & meta descriptions
covers.body: Written to earn the click, not just include the keyword.

covers.title: Headings & structure
covers.body: A heading hierarchy that mirrors how people scan and how search engines extract answers.

covers.title: Internal linking
covers.body: Contextual links that pass relevance and authority to the pages that need it.

useCases.body: Using Search Console to find pages ranking in positions 8–20 and improving them before creating anything new.

useCases.title: Service page rewrites
useCases.body: Restructuring service pages around the questions buyers ask before they enquire.

faqs.q: Is on-page SEO still important?
faqs.a: Yes. Links and technical health matter, but the page itself still has to be the most relevant answer. On-page work is often the fastest lever because you control it completely.

faqs.q: Will you rewrite all our content?
faqs.a: Rarely. Most gains come from targeted changes — structure, intent alignment, missing sections and better titles — on the pages with the most potential.

faqs.q: How do you choose which pages to optimise first?
faqs.a: Pages with existing impressions and rankings close to page one usually come first, weighted by how close each page sits to revenue.

ctaLine: Pages ranking, but not high enough?

name: Content SEO
summary: Content strategy, topical authority, briefs and SERP analysis — publishing what your market searches for, in an order that builds authority.
heroTitle: Content that's planned around search demand, not the editorial calendar.
heroIntro: Publishing more doesn't build authority. Publishing the right topics, in the right order, connected in the right way, does. I build content strategies your team can execute and briefs your writers can actually use.
problem: A lot of company blogs are a list of unrelated posts. Each one gets a burst of social traffic and then nothing, because none of them build towards a topic Google trusts the site on.
Content SEO means mapping the questions your buyers ask across the whole journey, then covering those topics more usefully than anyone else ranking today.

faqs.q: How much content do we need to publish?
faqs.a: Less than most people think. A consistent cadence of genuinely useful pages beats high volume. The topical map tells us how much ground there is to cover.

faqs.q: Can AI-written content rank?

heroIntro: Links still shape how much Google trusts a site. I focus on earning relevant links from real publications and partners, and on making sure the authority you already have reaches the pages that need it.
problem: Cheap link packages create risk and rarely move rankings in competitive markets. What moves them is relevance: links from sites your audience reads, pointing to pages that deserve them.
Before building anything, it's worth knowing the gap. Sometimes a site doesn't need more links — it needs its existing authority routed to money pages.

problem: Local rankings depend on proximity, relevance and prominence. You can't move your address, but you can control how relevant and prominent your business looks to Google.
Many businesses have an incomplete Business Profile, inconsistent contact details across the web, and one generic service page trying to rank in every area they serve.

problem: A good reputation offline does not always translate into visibility online. If competitors appear for your core services while your website relies on one generic page, homeowners may never discover your business.

More traffic is only useful when it brings the right jobs. I build an SEO plan around your service area, profitable services and capacity, then connect search visibility to qualified calls and quote requests so you can see what is working.

faqs.q: Which home service businesses do you work with?
faqs.a: This service is designed for plumbers, HVAC companies, electricians, roofers, septic providers, cleaners, landscapers, pest control businesses and other contractors. The strategy is tailored to the services and areas your team actually covers.

faqs.q: How is this different from general local SEO?
faqs.a: Local SEO is part of the work. Home service SEO also considers individual job types, emergency versus planned demand, seasonal services, coverage limits and the website experience that turns a homeowner search into a useful enquiry.

faqs.q: Can you help with Google Business Profile and my website?
faqs.a: Yes. I review how your profile and website support each other, then prioritise profile improvements, service pages, area pages and technical fixes. The implementation scope is agreed before the work begins.

faqs.q: Do I need a page for every town I serve?
faqs.a: No. Start with the areas that matter to your business and where you can provide useful, distinct information. Pages should reflect real service availability and local experience rather than repeating the same content with a different town name.

faqs.q: How long does home service SEO take to show results?
faqs.a: Timing depends on your starting point, local competition and how quickly changes are implemented. We establish a baseline and review progress over the following months. I do not guarantee a ranking position or a fixed number of leads.

faqs.q: How will we measure whether the SEO is working?
faqs.a: We agree on useful business measures such as qualified calls, quote requests and booked-job data where available. Organic traffic, page performance and local visibility provide context; lead quality helps decide the next priorities.

faqs.q: Can SEO work alongside paid ads?
faqs.a: Yes. SEO can build discovery through service pages and local search while ads address immediate demand. We can use enquiry data from both channels to understand which services and locations deserve more attention.

faqs.q: What do you need to get started?
faqs.a: Your website URL, core services, coverage areas and growth priorities are enough for an initial discussion. For the audit, access to Search Console, analytics and Google Business Profile helps identify the most useful next steps.

ctaLine: Ready to turn local searches into your next booked job?

faqs.q: Should product descriptions be unique?

problem: The common failure mode is the wrong country version ranking: UK visitors landing on US pricing, or an English page outranking the Arabic one in the UAE.

faqs.q: Subfolders or ccTLDs?
faqs.a: Subfolders consolidate authority and are easier to manage; ccTLDs send the strongest country signal but need their own authority. Most growing businesses start with subfolders.

faqs.q: Do we need hreflang for one language across several countries?
faqs.a: If content differs by country — pricing, availability, spelling — yes. If it's truly identical, you may not need separate versions at all.

faqs.q: Should we auto-redirect by location?
faqs.a: Generally no. Suggest the right version with a banner instead. Forced redirects can stop search engines crawling other versions.

faqs.q: What access do you need?
faqs.a: Search Console, analytics and ideally CMS access. Log files and a staging environment help for larger technical reviews.

faqs.q: How is this different from a free audit tool?
faqs.a: Tools find symptoms. An audit connects them to your data and goals, filters out noise and decides what to do first.

faqs.q: Can you help implement the roadmap?
faqs.a: Yes. Many audits turn into ongoing work, but the roadmap is written so your team can execute it independently too.

name: Keyword Research
summary: Mapping the searches your buyers make at every stage, sized by demand and ranked by business value and difficulty.
heroTitle: Keyword research that starts with your buyers, not a volume column.
heroIntro: The keywords worth targeting are the ones that bring the right people at the right moment. I map searches across the buyer journey and prioritise them by intent, business value and how realistically you can rank.
problem: High-volume keywords are tempting and usually the wrong place to start. They're competitive, vague in intent and often far from a purchase.
Low-volume, high-intent searches — comparisons, alternatives, specific use cases — frequently convert far better and are more winnable.

faqs.q: Is search volume reliable?
faqs.a: It's an estimate, often rounded and lagging. I use it for relative sizing and combine it with Search Console data, which reflects real impressions.

faqs.q: Should we target zero-volume keywords?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Tools under-report niche B2B searches. If sales conversations show people ask it, it's worth a page.

faqs.q: How often should keyword research be updated?
faqs.a: Revisit priorities quarterly and do a full refresh yearly or when the product or market changes.

name: Competitor SEO Research
summary: Understanding who wins your most valuable searches, how they do it, and where the openings are for you.
heroTitle: Competitor research that finds the openings, not just the gaps.
heroIntro: Your search competitors aren't always your business competitors. I identify who actually ranks for the searches that matter, break down why, and find the angles where you can win.
problem: Copying a competitor's content plan puts you permanently one step behind. The goal is to understand their strengths well enough to find what they're missing.
Often the real competition is a publisher, marketplace or review site — which changes the strategy entirely.

faqs.q: Who counts as an SEO competitor?
faqs.a: Any site ranking for the searches you want — including publishers, directories and marketplaces, not just direct business rivals.

faqs.q: Is it okay to create comparison pages about competitors?
faqs.a: Yes, if they're accurate and fair. Honest comparisons build trust and convert well; misleading ones backfire.

faqs.q: How often should competitors be reviewed?
faqs.a: Keep light monitoring monthly and do a deeper review every six months or after big market changes.
